Alford gives a careful definition of the Parable as a distinct literary form: unlike the Fable, it stays strictly within the bounds of natural probability rather than using talking animals or fanciful devices; unlike Myth, the vehicle and the thing conveyed are always distinguishable, even to a simple hearer; unlike Proverb (of which it is, rather, an expansion), it develops one particular case at length; and unlike Allegory, its persons and actions remain strictly themselves, typical of higher things by analogy rather than standing as transparent disguises for the realities meant. The Parable draws its power from real analogies impressed by the Creator on His own creation — hence only Christ, who made man and knows what is in him, can truly teach by parables without risk of perverting rather than guiding. The seven parables of this chapter form a single connected discourse (confirmed by ver. 53), not a later editorial collection: the first four spoken from the boat to the crowd, the last three to the disciples alone in the house.
13:3: vv. 3–9. The Sower. Mark iv. 2–9; Luke viii. 4–8 (see explanation at vv. 19–23).
13:4: 4. παρὰ τὴν ὁδόν — along the footpath running through the field.
13:5: 5, 6. τὰ πετρώδη — rocky ground where the native limestone, common in Palestine, lies just beneath a thin covering of soil; the radiated heat from the rock causes quick germination but, lacking depth for roots, equally quick withering.
13:7: 7, 8. The thorns are ground already containing the roots of thistles or briars, which choke the young plant as it grows alongside them.
13:10: vv. 10–17. Why Our Lord Taught in Parables. Mark iv. 10–12; Luke viii. 9, 10 (abridged). This question arose during a pause in teaching, not after entering the house (ver. 36) — its newness to the disciples shows this was the first deliberate, sustained use of parabolic teaching as such.
13:11: 11. The Kingdom of Heaven, like other kingdoms, has its inner secrets (μυστήριον, cf. Rom. xvi. 25 f.) reserved for those nearest its King — revealed to attentive, humble hearers, withheld (in the form of plain explanation) from the merely curious crowd.
13:12: 12. This saying sums up the double function of the parable: to the one who truly hears and understands, more is given (the parable's deeper revelation); from the one with no genuine spiritual desire, even the dim, confused notions he already has are further darkened by teaching whose depths he cannot penetrate enough even to recognize they exist. Alford finds striking confirmation of this principle's second half in the German rationalist commentators of his own day, and of its first half in commentators like Olshausen, Neander, Stier, and Trench.
13:13: 13. Matthew's 'because seeing they see not' and Mark/Luke's 'so that seeing they may not see' are not contradictory but two views of the same deep reality, both summed up already in ver. 12: he who lacks receptivity does not see, and what he seems to have is taken from him — these are simply two ways of stating one truth, not a fatalistic decree but a description of consequence.
13:14: 14, 15. This Isaiah citation (vi. 9, 10) is being progressively fulfilled in stages, of which a partial fulfillment already occurred among the prophet's own contemporaries — quoted verbatim from the LXX, which renders the Hebrew imperative ('make the heart of this people fat') as indicative, without changing the sense. This citation gives no support to a fatalist reading: the entire blame rests on the settled hard-heartedness of the hearers themselves, which makes even the very preaching of the word a further occasion of darkening and condemnation (cf. 2 Cor. iv. 3, 4).
13:16: 16, 17. A saying repeated, in slightly different form, at Luke x. 23, 24 — likely a teaching our Lord used on more than one occasion. On prophets and righteous men longing to see what the disciples now see, cf. 2 Sam. xxiii. 5; Job xix. 23–27.
13:18: vv. 18–23. Interpretation of the Parable of the Sower. Mark iv. 10–20; Luke viii. 9–18. The parable's central idea is that the grace of God and human receptivity to it always work together: the seed is one and the same everywhere, but it cannot spring up without suitable soil, just as soil cannot bring forth without seed — though the deeper question of why one soil differs from another leads, on the spiritual side, into the inscrutable, sovereign workings of the God who 'preventeth us that we may have a good will, and worketh with us when we have that will' (Article X, Church of England).
13:19: 19. The sower is first the Son of Man Himself (ver. 37), then His ministers after Him (cf. 1 Cor. iii. 6) — sowing indiscriminately over every kind of ground, as He commands His own sowers to do (Mark xvi. 15); the parable describes only His sowing, not His economy, and is not undermined by the objection that a careful farmer would not waste seed on bad soil, since that is simply outside the parable's intended scope (Stier). The 'one sown by the wayside' (not merely 'one who received seed') reflects a deeper identity: the sown seed itself, taking root or failing to, *becomes* the person described, exactly as believers are said to be 'born again of the living word of God' (1 Pet. i. 23).
13:20: 20, 21. In this second case the surface of the mind is easily stirred but the deeper heart remains harder than the trodden path; πρόσκαιρός ἐστιν conveys both 'lasts only a while' and 'is governed entirely by circumstance.'
13:22: 22. In this third case everything about the soil is favorable except for one thing — fruitfulness is prevented by a divided will, a half-service (μέριμνα, from μερίζω, 'to divide,' as at ch. vi. 25) that always ends with evil overcoming good. Alford stresses that πλοῦτος in Scripture is not wealth as objectively possessed but wealth as subjectively desired and valued — this class is not limited to the literally rich.
13:23: 23. Alford traces a threefold progression among the unfruitful classes — in time (failure at the very outset, soon after growth, or after maturity), in apparent degree (an ascending climax from not understanding, to understanding-and-feeling, to understanding-feeling-and-practicing), yet in real degree the reverse (worse and worse) — while cautioning that none of the four classes are meant as sharply walled-off categories excluding the others; the same person may, at different times, exhibit traits of more than one. The good soil itself is not naturally good but made receptive by grace alone — the parable describes no innately superior class of persons, only the differing operation of grace amid differing dispositions. The varying yields (hundred-, sixty-, thirtyfold) represent differing degrees of faithfulness and devotion among those who do bear fruit, unlike the parable of the talents, where unequal initial gifts yield proportionally equal commendation.
13:24: vv. 24–30. The Tares of the Field (peculiar to Matthew; explained at vv. 36–43). ὡμοιώθη... ἀνθρώπῳ means 'is like the whole case of a man...,' not a strict one-to-one comparison of the kingdom itself to a man.
13:25: 25. ζιζάνια — almost certainly darnel (bastard wheat), which closely resembles young wheat and only becomes distinguishable once it comes into ear — explaining why the tares 'appeared' only later. Alford notes (from his own first-hand observation as editor, citing a real incident on his own land in Leicestershire) that malicious sowing of weeds over a neighbor's planted field, as a deliberate act of revenge, is an attested Eastern practice and not unknown even in 19th-century England.
13:27: 27–29. Jerome, writing from personal experience in Palestine, notes that darnel and wheat are nearly indistinguishable while still green, which is why the householder forbids premature uprooting — the risk of damaging the wheat is too great until harvest makes the distinction clear.
13:31: vv. 31, 32. The Grain of Mustard Seed. Mark iv. 30–34; Luke xiii. 18, 19. Chrysostom notes the connexion with the preceding parables: having just shown how much of the sown seed is lost (the tares, and even within what survives, real loss), lest the disciples despair at how few might prove faithful, our Lord now reassures them with the image of inevitable, eventual large-scale growth from the smallest of beginnings.
13:32: 32. μικρότερον ('less than all') — not a strict superlative but the standard Jewish proverbial type for extreme smallness; Lightfoot cites Rabbinic sources attesting that mustard plants in Palestine genuinely grew to a remarkable size, tree-like and climbable. Alford traces a double application: (1) generally, to the outwardly insignificant beginnings of the Kingdom (the manger at Bethlehem, the crucified Christ, the 120 names of Acts i.) growing into a worldwide reality — with the important caution that the outward institutional Church is not itself this growing plant, but rather, where uncorrupted, may serve and shelter it, much as scaffolding serves a building under construction; (2) individually, to the small beginnings of grace in a single soul — a word, a thought, a passing impression that eventually fills and shelters the whole inner life. Jerome's comment is notable: measured against the great philosophical systems of the world by purely literary or rhetorical standards, the Gospel's proclamation is the least and humblest of all teachings — yet alone among them it grows, not into mere herbs that soon wither, but into a tree.
13:33: 33. The Leaven. Luke xiii. 20, 21. Alford firmly rejects readings that take 'leaven' here in its usual negative biblical sense (corruption, as at ch. xvi. 6; 1 Cor. v. 6, 7) and so read the parable as describing the Church's gradual corruption: the grammar parallels the mustard-seed parable exactly (the kingdom is like the leaven itself, not like the whole resulting process of corruption), and such a reading would also flatly contradict the parable's evident purpose, paired as it is with the previous one, of illustrating healthy, beneficial growth. The two parables are intimately related: the mustard seed illustrates the Kingdom's own inherent power of self-expansion; the leaven, its power of penetrating and transforming a foreign mass entirely unlike itself, until the whole is assimilated — with the added detail that ordinary leaven is itself a piece of a previously-leavened loaf, exactly as the Kingdom is the renewal of humanity through the one righteous Man, Christ Jesus. As with the mustard seed, the application is both corporate (the gradual transformation of whole societies — Alford instances, from his own century, the abandonment of slavery and dueling and the growing revulsion at war among Christian nations) and individual (the mystery of regeneration and ongoing sanctification in a single soul).
13:34: 34, 35. Conclusion of the Parables to the Multitude. Mark iv. 33, 34. The citation (Ps. lxxviii. 2, attributed to Asaph) is fully appropriate, against De Wette's objection that the Psalm itself 'contains no parable' — the whole Psalm is precisely the kind of typological historical recounting Paul says was 'written for our admonition' (1 Cor. x. 6, 11).
13:36: vv. 36–43. Interpretation of the Parable of the Tares (peculiar to Matthew). 38. The field is the world — and if understood of the Church at all, only as the Church is coextensive with the whole world (cf. Mark xvi. 15, 'preach the gospel to every creature') — THE CHURCH standing for THE WORLD, not the reverse. Alford traces the parable's primary references: (1) to the whole sweep of history from the entrance of sin to the final judgment, with the Lord here gathering the entire span of human history into the compass of a single sowing and a single harvest; (2) more specifically to the Kingdom of Heaven beginning with the Incarnation — the Gospel sowing only good seed, all corruption being the Enemy's separate, additional work (already visible as early as Acts v.; cf. Paul's naming of Elymas as 'son of the devil,' Acts xiii. 10). Alford stresses (3) that the line between 'wheat' and 'tares' is not fixed once for all during the present probationary period — individuals are not consigned irrevocably to one class or the other until the final harvest, since God 'willeth not the death of a sinner.' He also notes (4) the parable's importance in the ancient Donatist controversy: the Donatists, claiming the Church must be a perfectly pure congregation, wrongly argued this parable did not apply to them since it speaks of 'the world,' missing the deeper point that the world itself, in this parable, simply *is* the field within which the true Church grows, intermixed with tares.
13:40: 40–43. τὰ σκάνδαλα — generally understood of persons who cause others to stumble (tempters, hinderers), though Stier suggests it may include things as well as the persons named just after. ἐκλάμψουσιν — 'shall shine out' (their present light here being dim and obscured), as the sun emerging from cloud — this final, sublime declaration about the righteous goes beyond the strict bounds of the parable's interpretation proper.
13:44: 44. The Hidden Treasure (peculiar to Matthew; closely paired with the following parable — both, like the seventh, addressed to the disciples alone, not the crowd). A man, perhaps laboring for someone else or passing by chance, discovers treasure hidden in a field and, overjoyed, sells all he has to buy the field itself, thereby (under Jewish law) becoming the legal owner of the treasure too. This pictures one who, without deliberately seeking it, unexpectedly finds within some branch of the visible Church the true treasure of saving faith — and, having found it, secures not the treasure in isolation (an impossibility) but the whole field (the outward means of grace in that branch of the Church) in order to keep it.
13:45: 45, 46. The Pearl of Great Price. Unlike the previous parable, here a merchant — one whose deliberate business and trained habit is the determined, discriminating search for fine pearls — represents the person who, from youth, has been earnestly and systematically seeking spiritual truth, and who at last, among many lesser treasures already found, discovers the one pearl of supreme worth: saving, vital faith itself, found not embedded within any outward institution but in its own purest, most direct form. Trench instances Nathanael and the Samaritan woman as examples of unexpected finders (parallel to the hidden treasure), and Augustine (or, Alford adds, Paul, cf. Phil. iii. 7) as an example of the diligent seeker who finds.
13:47: vv. 47–50. The Dragnet (peculiar to Matthew). σαγήνη — a large drag-net swept along the sea bottom, catching everything in its path. The leading idea is the final separation of holy and unholy within the visible Church for the Master's use; notably, the fishermen themselves are never mentioned — the comparison does not extend to them. The net, gathering of every kind from the sea (a common Scripture figure for the nations, cf. Rev. xvii. 15), is drawn to shore (the σuvτέλεια, the close of the age) only at the very end, where the angels — explicitly distinguished from the net's gatherers, just as in the tares parable the servants and reapers were kept distinct — perform the final separation.
13:51:
51, 52. Solemn Conclusion of the Parables. When the disciples answer 'Yea, Lord' to whether they have understood, this must be read from their own limited, then-current standpoint, not as full comprehension of the deeper meaning the Holy Spirit would later unfold to them. Every γραμματεύς ('scribe') instructed in the Kingdom of Heaven is compared to a householder bringing out from his store both new things and old — i.e., the disciples themselves, as they grow in understanding, will continually draw fresh as well as familiar meaning from these very sayings; and this remains true of every genuinely spiritually-taught interpreter of Scripture in every age, drawing not merely from books or learning but from his own store of living, experiential knowledge of the word.

Alford closes with extended reflections on the seven parables as a unified whole: their imagery arises naturally from the actual surroundings before our Lord as He taught (the fertile plain of Gennesaret, the footpaths, the rocky outcrops, the thorny waste ground, all visible from the boat); the seven together form one coherent meditation moving from the first sowing of the Church to its final consummation; while resisting attempts (as in some older commentators) to assign each parable mechanically to a specific historical period of Church history, Alford allows that, taken as a whole, the cycle does broadly trace the Church's history from its apostolic sowing, through the early heresies (tares), its gradual worldwide growth (mustard seed) and quiet inward transformation of society (leaven), through ages of denominational division in which individuals nonetheless find the hidden treasure and the pearl of price, to the final, all-encompassing day of separation.
13:53: vv. 53–58. Teaching and Rejection at Nazareth. Mark vi. 1–6; cf. Luke iv. 16–29. Alford notes that the events of ch. viii. 18–ix. 34 may belong chronologically between these two verses, given Mark's apparent same-day connection of the storm-stilling and the parables discourse.
13:55: 55, 56. The Brethren of the Lord. Alford devotes an extensive excursus to this famously disputed question, working strictly from the N.T. evidence itself rather than later tradition. His conclusions: (1) there were four men consistently called 'his brethren' (James/Jacob, Joseph/Joses, Simon, Judas), distinct from the Twelve Apostles (explicitly excluded by John vii. 5, since at least two of them — James and Jude — are elsewhere associated with apostleship in ways that, on close examination, do not place them among the original Twelve); (2) in every Gospel mention except John vii., they appear directly alongside Mary, exactly as her own literal sons would; (3) nothing in the text gives any warrant for reading 'brethren' here as anything other than the plain, literal sense in which 'his mother' is plainly literal. Alford rejects both major traditional alternatives — that they were sons of Alphæus/Clopas and so cousins (which conflicts with at least one, possibly several, of that Alphæus's sons being explicitly among the Twelve, and explicitly *not* among the unbelieving brethren of John vii. 5), and that they were Joseph's children by an earlier marriage (for which Scripture offers no support whatsoever, no other mother ever being named). He stresses, against later objectors, that accepting these as Mary's own literal children carries no implication whatsoever regarding the miraculous conception of Jesus — the virgin conception and Mary's life thereafter being, in his view, entirely separate questions (cf. note at ch. i. 25).
13:57: 57, 58. The proverb about a prophet's lack of honor in his own country is fulfilled in Nazareth's unbelief, which in turn limited (though did not entirely prevent) the miracles performed there — Alford takes the limitation as a real, not merely apparent, consequence of their unbelief, consistent with the general principle that miracles, throughout the Gospels, presuppose rather than coerce faith.
14:1: vv. 1–12. Herod Hears of Jesus; the Death of John the Baptist (told in retrospect). Mark vi. 14–29; Luke ix. 7–9 (who omits John's death). This was Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great by Malthace, tetrarch of Galilee and Peræa, who divorced the daughter of King Aretas of Arabia to take Herodias, wife of his half-brother Herod Philip — a step that eventually provoked a disastrous war with Aretas (which the Jews, per Josephus, attributed to divine vengeance for John's death) and ended in Antipas's banishment by Caligula.
14:2: 2. αὐτός is emphatic: 'it is *he*.' Luke records Herod as perplexed rather than asserting this outright himself — no real inconsistency, since the rumor began with others, but Herod's own guilty conscience evidently led him to voice the same conclusion. Alford notes there is no evidence Herod was a Sadducee or skeptical of resurrection generally; this is a genuine belief in actual bodily resurrection (not metempsychosis), and incidentally confirms John x. 41 (that John himself performed no miracle in life, hence the supposed new power must come from having passed through death).
14:4: 4. Alford lays out the threefold illegality of Antipas's marriage, drawing directly on Josephus: (1) Herodias's first husband (Philip) was still living; (2) Antipas's own first wife (daughter of Aretas) was also still living; (3) Antipas and Herodias were already related within forbidden degrees (Lev. xviii. 16), since Herodias's father Aristobulus was brother to both Antipas and Philip.
14:5: 5. Per Mark's fuller account, Herod actually feared John, knowing him to be righteous and holy, protected him, and heard him gladly even while keeping him imprisoned — Josephus, unaware of these deeper religious grounds, attributes the imprisonment to purely political motives (Herod's fear of John's popular influence).
14:6: 6. γενεσίοις — 'birthday,' though the word originally denoted, in classical Greek, an anniversary commemoration of the dead; by later Greek usage (attested in Josephus and elsewhere) it had also come to mean a literal birthday celebration, as clearly intended here. The dancing girl was Salome, daughter of Herodias by her first husband Philip — who later married her uncle Philip the tetrarch, and afterward her cousin Aristobulus.
14:9: 9. ὁ βασιλεύς — a title Herod Antipas never actually possessed (he was only tetrarch); Herodias later pressed him to seek it formally from Rome, a venture that ended instead in his exile. Per Mark vi. 20, Herod's grief was genuine, since he had heard John gladly.
14:10: 10. The feast was evidently held at or near Machærus, the frontier fortress where John was imprisoned.
14:13: vv. 13–21. Feeding of the Five Thousand. Mark vi. 30–44; Luke ix. 10–17; John vi. 1–13. Alford reconciles the apparent immediacy of cause-and-effect between hearing of John's death and withdrawing, with the parenthetical, retrospective placement of the death narrative, by noting the news likely took several days to travel from Machærus, and that 'at that time' (ver. 1) itself covers a fairly broad span. Jesus's withdrawal was also tied to the return of the Twelve from their mission (cf. Mark vi. 30–35).
14:15: 15. This 'evening' is the earlier one, the decline of day (around 3 p.m.); the 'evening' of ver. 23, after the miracle, is late at night.
14:16: 16, 17. John's fuller account (vi. 3–7) identifies Andrew as the disciple who spoke, and a boy as the source of the five barley loaves and two fish. Alford notes a similar earlier miracle at 2 Kings iv. 42–44 (Elisha feeding a hundred men with twenty barley loaves) as a suggestive precedent.
14:19: 19. ηὐλόγησεν — Luke supplies 'them' (the loaves and fish) as object; John has 'having given thanks' — both describe the same act, thanks to heaven constituting the blessing on the food. Alford, citing Meyer, conceives the mechanics of the miracle thus: the Lord blessed and distributed the loaves and fish as they were, and the miraculous multiplication occurred *during* the disciples' ongoing distribution, so that there proved to be enough for all. He notes the symbolic resonance for the Twelve, just returned from their mission under the charge 'freely ye have received, freely give' (ch. x. 8).
14:20: 20. κοφίνους — the small wicker basket proverbially carried by Jews (cf. Juvenal's mocking reference to 'the Jew, whose furniture is a basket and some hay'), traditionally explained as used to carry their own food while traveling, to avoid ritual defilement from Gentile food.
14:22: vv. 22–33. Jesus Walks on the Sea. Mark vi. 45–52; John vi. 16–21 (Luke omits this episode). Following the feeding, the crowd's conviction that Jesus was the Messiah led them to attempt to seize and crown Him by force (John vi. 14, 15) — our Lord's urgent dismissal of the disciples was therefore an important step in defusing this premature, politically-charged enthusiasm, since the disciples themselves were likely all too sympathetic to the crowd's intent.
14:25: 25. The fourth watch, by the Roman reckoning by then common among the Jews (who themselves traditionally divided the night into three watches), falls between roughly 3 and 6 a.m.
14:26: 26, 27. The phrase 'walking on the sea' (common to all three Synoptic accounts) can mean nothing other than that our Lord literally, bodily walked on the water's surface — Alford rejects attempts to soften this via a supposed idiom for 'walking on the shore,' noting that all the cited parallel usages of that construction occur with verbs of rest, not of motion, and so do not apply here.
14:28: vv. 28–31. Peter Walks on the Water (peculiar to Matthew). Strikingly consistent with Peter's characteristically warm, impulsive, overconfident temperament — Alford notes it has been called almost a 'rehearsal' of his later denial — and offers one of the most pointed scriptural illustrations of the nature of faith: bold at the outset, but failing under the pressure of circumstance once the eye shifts from Christ to the visible danger.
15:1: vv. 1–20. Discourse on Defilement. Mark vii. 1–23. The challenge comes from scribes and Pharisees sent from Jerusalem.
15:3: 3. The καί implies a reciprocal charge: 'and you, for your part, transgress the commandment of God...' ἡ ἐντολὴ τοῦ θεοῦ is a notable testimony from our Lord to the divine origin of the Mosaic law generally, not merely the Decalogue (the second commandment cited, honoring parents and the death penalty for cursing them, technically falls outside the Ten Words proper) — note also that where Matthew has 'God commanded,' Mark has 'Moses said,' treating the two as equivalent.
15:5: 5, 6. Lightfoot shows that the formula our Lord cites did not necessarily bind the speaker to actually consecrate the property to religious use — the mere utterance of it (the Corban formula, cf. Mark vii. 11) was sufficient by itself to release him from the duty of supporting his parents, a legal technicality that the Pharisees' tradition exploited to override the plain commandment.
15:8: 8, 9. The Isaiah passage cited (xxix. 13) belongs to a larger section (chs. xxiv–xxxv) of alternating threats and promises directed at nominal versus true Israel — as so often in prophecy, the immediate historical reference is only one instance of a deeper, recurring pattern in God's dealings with His people across every age.
15:10: 10. Euthymius: 'having silenced and shamed [the Pharisees], He leaves them as past cure, and turns His word instead to the multitude, as more worthy of it.'
15:12: 12. This exchange occurred after entering the house, apart from the crowd (cf. Mark vii. 17).
15:13: 13. The 'plant' is the Pharisees' own merely human teaching, not of divine planting — confirmed by the following 'let them alone,' and consistent with our Lord's regular parabolic pattern of identifying seed/plant with doctrine that becomes embodied in its teachers and followers. Bengel: φυτόν = nature (the plant itself), φυτεία = the cultivating, the planting.
15:15: 15. The saying in ver. 11, though strictly a plain declaration rather than a parable in the technical sense, is here called a παραβολή in the wider sense of 'a difficult saying' — Stier suggests their habit of asking for explanations of true parables in ch. xiii. had carried over into this looser usage of the term for any hard saying.
15:16: 16. Since ver. 11 was originally addressed to the crowd with the charge 'hear and understand,' the disciples — who should have grasped it more readily still — are gently rebuked for their continued obtuseness. ἀκμήν ('still,' 'even now') is a distinctly later Greek usage.
15:17: 17, 18. Philo offers a striking philosophical parallel: the mouth is, as Plato said, the 'entrance and exit' for what is mortal — food and drink (perishable nourishment for a perishable body) enter, while words — the immortal laws of an immortal soul, by which the rational life is governed — go out.
15:21: vv. 21–28. The Canaanite Woman. Mark vii. 24–30 (omitted by Luke). Alford judges, from Matthew's consistent usage of εἰς τὰ μέρη elsewhere in this Gospel (always implying actual entrance into a region, not merely approach to its border), that our Lord did in fact cross the frontier into Gentile territory — though the point is not of great importance, since He went there not to teach or heal but, evidently, to escape the rising hostility of the Pharisees for a time (cf. Mark's account, which implies He wished to remain hidden and could not).
15:22: 22. The woman is called 'Canaanite' by descent, though Mark identifies her religiously as 'Greek' (i.e., a pagan) and ethnically as 'Syro-Phoenician.' It was her *descent*, not her place of residence, that placed the customary barrier between her and Israel's Messiah; her use of 'Son of David' shows real familiarity with Jewish messianic expectation, telling against De Wette's suggestion that she was merely a proselyte.
15:23: 23. The disciples' request to 'send her away' must be read together with Mark's note that our Lord wished not to be recognized — meaning, roughly, 'she is drawing everyone's attention to us'; ἀπόλυσον itself does not specify whether her request should be granted or refused, only that she should be dismissed somehow, leaving the method to our Lord.
15:24: 24. Cf. ch. x. 5–6: this defines the scope of our Lord's personal earthly ministry, yet even this rule was, as here, occasionally and graciously overridden — 'the sealed fountain' breaking its banks as a foretaste of the wider grace soon to follow (cf. Rom. xv. 8).
15:26: 26. κυναρίοις — the diminutive here indicates no special contempt beyond the ordinary use of 'dogs' for Gentiles, and certainly no slight directed at the woman's daughter; diminutives in this idiom often express familiarity, as for household pets rather than scavenging street dogs.
15:27: 27. The woman, in true humility, accepts the very term our Lord uses and turns it into the ground of her plea: 'Yes, Lord — for even the little dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table.' She positions herself, as it were, just under the edge of Israel's table, at its very threshold.
15:28: 28. The greatness of her faith lay precisely in this: that in the face of repeated discouragement she persisted, and even turned the very objections raised against her into fresh grounds for her plea. Mark adds that on returning home she found her daughter already healed, lying calmly on the bed.
15:29: vv. 29–39. Healing by the Sea of Galilee (peculiar to Matthew; cf. Mark vii. 31–37) and the Feeding of the Four Thousand (Mark viii. 1–10). τὸ ὄρος is simply the high ground along the lakeshore, not a specific named mountain; per Mark vii. 31 this was on the eastern, Decapolis side of the lake.
15:30: 30. κυλλοί — those maimed or disabled in the hands (sometimes also the feet); the healing need not imply the literal regrowth of a missing limb, only the cure of a disabling injury or paralysis. ἔρριψαν — 'cast down,' not from neglect but from eager haste.
15:31: 31. Alford suggests the disciples' own joy may be reflected in the added phrase 'the God of Israel' — a contrast, consciously or not, with the recent difficulty of the Canaanite Gentile woman's faith in obtaining help, now set against this abundant outpouring of mercy on Israel itself.
15:32: vv. 32–39. The Feeding of the Four Thousand. Alford firmly rejects the German rationalist claim that this is merely a doublet of the feeding of the five thousand (ch. xiv): every circumstance that *could* differ between the two accounts does differ (the occasion, the proportions, the precise wording), and decisively, the type of basket used to collect the leftover fragments is consistently distinguished in the Greek across both Gospel accounts — κόφινοι at the first miracle, σπυρίδες at the second — a level of consistency, Alford argues, no plausible later interpolator or careless duplicator could have maintained, and confirmed beyond doubt by our Lord's own later explicit reference to both as two separate events (ch. xvi. 9, 10).
15:37: 37. σπυρίς — a large basket, big enough to hold a man's body (cf. Paul lowered from the Damascus wall in one, Acts ix. 25) — considerably larger than the κόφινος of the earlier miracle.
15:39: 39. Of Magadan/Magdala little certain is known; most travelers place it a few miles from Tiberias on the west side of the lake, at a site now called Madschel — Dalmanutha (Mark's parallel name) was likely a neighboring village.
16:1: vv. 1–4. Request for a Sign from Heaven. Mark viii. 11–13 (much abridged); cf. Luke xii. 54. Alford sees no reason to identify this with the earlier demand at ch. xii. 38: nothing more natural than that hostile questioners would repeat such a challenge on more than one occasion. Jewish superstition held that demons and false gods could produce signs *on earth*, but only the true God could give a sign *from heaven* — hence the specific, pointed nature of this demand (cf. the precedents alleged: manna, Joshua's sun, Samuel's thunder, Elijah's fire).
16:2: 2, 3. A genuine weather proverb of the time (cf. similar Greco-Roman folk-meteorology in Pliny), used by our Lord to draw out the irony: they read the sky's signs skillfully enough, yet are blind to the unmistakable signs of their own historic moment — Alford notes the scepter had by now departed from Judah, the line of native rulers had ended, and Daniel's prophetic weeks were nearing their close, yet none of this registered with them.
16:4: See ch. xii. 39 for the sign of Jonah.
16:5: vv. 5–12. Warning against the Leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. Mark viii. 13–21. This crossing is distinct from the earlier voyage to Magadan (ch. xv. 39) — Mark notes our Lord re-embarked specifically after this dialogue. ἐπελάθοντο — they forgot, after landing, to provide bread for their onward journey (not a pluperfect, 'had forgotten' before embarking).
16:6: 6. The comparison draws on leaven's penetrating, diffusive quality (cf. ch. xiii. 33), whether for good or ill; in the parallel saying at Luke xii. 1 (a different occasion) the leaven is explicitly identified as hypocrisy — the charge our Lord most frequently brings against the Jewish sects. Mark adds 'the leaven of Herod' — the Herodians being a chiefly political rather than religious faction, mostly Sadducean in belief, united with the Pharisees in opposing Christ despite their mutual hostility, sharing the same underlying leaven of hypocrisy and unbelief.
16:8: 8–12. The disciples had forgotten not only the two feeding miracles themselves but the weightier lesson just given at ch. xv. 16–20 about the source of true defilement.
16:13:
vv. 13–20. Peter's Confession. Mark viii. 27–30; Luke ix. 18–21 (where Luke rejoins the Synoptic narrative). This marks the beginning of the second great division of the Lord's earthly ministry — the turn toward His sufferings and death — paralleling how the first period opened with the Father's declared testimony to His Sonship at the baptism, just as this new period will soon be marked similarly at the Transfiguration.

Καισαρείας τῆς Φιλίππου — a town in Gaulonitis at the foot of Mount Lebanon near the source of the Jordan, anciently Laish/Dan, later Paneas (from Mount Panium); enlarged and renamed Cæsarea by the tetrarch Philip — to be distinguished from the coastal Cæsarea Stratonis of Acts.

τίνα λέγουσιν... τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου — Alford defends the reading 'the Son of Man' (rather than the variant 'me') as both better attested and theologically richer: a 'pregnant expression' which even then carried, in popular and especially disciple understanding, implications of the title's full Messianic and divine weight (cf. Luke xxii. 69, 70) — setting up exactly the kind of open-ended test of the disciples' own developing faith that the following question requires.
16:14: 14. No real contradiction with those who elsewhere called Him 'Son of David' (ch. ix. 27; xii. 23; xv. 22) — those were either disciples, examples of unusual faith, or, as in ch. xii. 23, only a passing, unsettled impression of the crowd, not a fixed popular verdict. On the Herod/John-the-Baptist theory, cf. ch. xiv. 2. Jeremiah was reckoned by the Jews as first among the prophetic books (Lightfoot).
16:16: 16. Chrysostom: 'who then is the mouth of the Apostles but Peter, ever fervent, the foremost of the apostolic band? When all are asked, he alone answers.' The confession's form — 'Thou art,' not 'we say' or 'I think' — marks it as the expression of an inward conviction wrought directly by God's Spirit. Its excellence lies in holding together both the human and divine natures: ὁ χριστός names the Messiah, the anointed Son of David; ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος names the Eternal Son in a sense entirely distinct from any merely honorific or angelic 'sonship' then current in Jewish Messianic expectation (which envisioned, per Justin Martyr, simply a man chosen by God for the office on account of his virtues, not a divine Person). Alford does not claim Peter grasped every later theological implication of his own words, only that they were a genuine, Spirit-given testimony to both the true humanity and true divinity of Christ.
16:17: 17. μακάριος here, as at ch. v. 4 etc., is a solemn pronouncement of blessing — inclusion in the kingdom of heaven — not mere praise; its ground is that the Father Himself revealed this to Peter (cf. ch. xi. 25–27). Alford notes Paul's language at Gal. i. 15, 16 ('flesh and blood') almost certainly echoes this very saying, Paul there implicitly claiming a comparable direct, divine — not human — origin for his own apostolic calling.
16:18:
18. The famous 'Rock' saying. Alford argues at length and decisively for Peter's own personal reference: the name Πέτρος was first given prophetically at his very first meeting with our Lord (John i. 43), and throughout the N.T. it is consistently *persons*, never doctrines or confessions in the abstract, who are called the pillars and stones of the spiritual building (cf. 1 Pet. ii. 4–6; Gal. ii. 9; Eph. ii. 20; Rev. iii. 12; xxi. 14). Peter, precisely as the one who, by direct divine revelation, made this confession, becomes the first of the foundation stones on which the Church was built — historically and literally fulfilled in his leading role in admitting first Jews (Acts ii) and then Gentiles (Acts x, xi) into the Church.

Yet Alford is equally emphatic that nothing in the promise supports any doctrine of perpetual papal succession: the promise concerns Peter the *person*, in his unique, unrepeatable historical role, not an office transmissible to successors — citing Bengel's blunt remark, 'these things are said of Peter; what have they to do with Rome?' He also firmly rejects the opposite extreme (Wordsworth's view that πέτρα must refer to Christ alone, excluding any reference to Πέτρος): 'let us keep to the plain, straightforward sense of Scripture, however that sense may have been misused by Rome' — there is, in his judgment, an unmistakable wordplay connecting Πέτρος and πέτρα that cannot honestly be denied.

μου before τὴν ἐκκλησίαν is simply ordinary Greek word order, carrying no special mystical weight (against Wordsworth's claim of solecism). πύλαι ᾅδου — 'the gates of Hades,' an Eastern idiom for the power of death itself; the promise that this power shall never finally prevail against the Church so founded.
16:19:
19. The Keys, and Binding and Loosing. A further, distinctly personal promise to Peter, remarkably fulfilled in his literal historical role opening the door of the Gospel to both Jews and Gentiles (and, conversely, his rebuke of Simon Magus as an instance of 'shutting,' Acts viii. 21). Alford insists grammatically that the shift to direct second-person address (καὶ δώσω σοί) cannot honestly be read as a mere continuation of a general statement rather than a renewed, personal address to Peter specifically.

'Binding and loosing' is repeated later (ch. xviii. 18) as a more general grant to all the disciples, though first and most prominently verified in Peter himself (Ananias and Sapphira as an instance of 'binding'; the healing at the Beautiful Gate as an instance of 'loosing'). Alford reads the phrase, per its Jewish background (Hebrew asar/hittir, 'forbid'/'permit'), as referring to the Apostles' legislative authority within the Church, not — against some — to literal forgiveness or retention of individual sins (since 'binding sins,' unlike 'loosing sins,' has no scriptural or linguistic precedent as a way of speaking of *retaining* guilt): it is the sinner, not the sin, that is properly said to be 'bound.'
16:20: See note at ch. viii. 4 on our Lord's general policy of restraining premature publicity about His Messiahship.
16:21: vv. 21–28. Our Lord Announces His Approaching Death and Resurrection; Rebuke of Peter. Mark viii. 31–ix. 1; Luke ix. 22–27. Earlier, only obscure hints of coming suffering (ch. x. 38; John iii. 14) and resurrection (John ii. 19) had been given; this is the first plain, explicit announcement. Mark adds the detail that He spoke this 'openly' (παρρησίᾳ).
16:22: 22. Alford rejects Schleiermacher's objection that it is psychologically improbable for Peter's noble confession and carnal rebuke to follow so closely together: in fact spiritual insight and carnal weakness frequently stand close together in the same person, and never more so than immediately after a moment of high commendation and exaltation, which can itself breed presumption. ἵλεώς σοι — 'God be merciful to thee' (i.e., may this never happen), a Hebraistic construction; οὐ μὴ ἔσται is not a wish but an authoritative, presumptuous *declaration* on Peter's part — as though he knew better and could guarantee his Master's safety against the divine purpose itself, which is exactly what draws the Lord's sharp rebuke.
16:23: 23. The very faculty that had just made Peter a foundation stone of the Church — Spirit-given discernment — when set against the will of God instead, now makes him an adversary: Alford notes the deliberate echo of ch. iv. 10, our Lord using on Peter the identical rebuke first given to Satan himself. σκάνδαλον εἶ ἐμοῦ — 'thou art *my* stumbling-block' (the emphatic, unarticulated noun thrust forward for stress), not merely 'a stumbling-block to me' — a striking, deliberate echo of πέτρος/πέτρα, since the same Peter who was just called the Church's foundation-stone now becomes, through carnal presumption, a stone of stumbling instead (cf. Peter's own later language at 1 Pet. ii. 7, 8).
16:24: vv. 24–28. A solemn sequel to the announcement of His own suffering and the rebuke of Peter: not only Christ but all His followers must suffer and deny themselves; all have a 'life' (in the deepest sense) to be saved, and a final day of reckoning for it. Cf. ch. x. 38, 39.
16:26: 26. Likely echoing Ps. xlix. (cf. esp. ver. 8 LXX). ψυχή here means not merely 'soul' but 'life' in its higher, ultimate sense — what could a man possibly offer in exchange to buy back such a life once forfeited?
16:27: 27. A further revelation in this pivotal chapter: the Son of Man is to be the universal Judge, appearing with His angels in His Father's glory (cf. ch. xiii. 41; xxiv. 30; xxv. 31) — Mark and Luke place a related saying (cf. ch. x. 33) at this point instead; Alford suggests our Lord likely joined both declarations together on this occasion.
16:28: 28. 'Some standing here shall not taste death till they see the Son of Man coming in His kingdom' — most naturally and immediately fulfilled, in Alford's reading, by the Transfiguration that follows in the very next chapter, a proleptic foretaste and visible pledge of that future glory.
